title: Vertex-Mounted Rhombus Ducts for Solar Air Heaters: Effect of Interior Angle on Heat Transfer, Friction, and Daily Air Temperature Rise
content: Most solar air heater ducts collect sunlight through a single flat absorber on top. A rhombus-shaped duct stood on one of its corners exposes two sloping faces to the sky instead, so one face can catch the low morning sun and the other the evening sun. This paper reviews the computational study of Dara et al., which varied the interior angle of such a duct from 40° to 140° in 10° steps. They used RNG k–ε simulations at Reynolds numbers of 5000–28,000, with unequal heat fluxes on the two faces to represent morning, noon, and evening sun. The 90° duct, which is a square turned on its corner, performed best. At Re = 28,000 it gave 17.24% more heat transfer and 7.3% more friction than the 40° duct, and the authors report an overall performance factor 20.6% higher. The air temperature rise was almost independent of angle and increased by about 60% from morning to noon. We add a geometric and energy-balance analysis of our own. It shows that the hydraulic diameter, the mass flow, and the heated area follow directly from the side length and the angle, and that angles θ and 180° − θ give the same cross-section rotated by 90°. It also shows that the 60% daily rise is exactly the ratio of total incident flux. Two reported figures, the 20.6% performance gain and the 1.85-fold advantage over a flat-mounted square duct, cannot be reproduced from the paper’s own data and need clarification. A simple sun-path estimate confirms that two faces catch about 1.6 times the daily beam energy of a flat duct of the same side, though much of that comes from the wider footprint.
